title: Death Penalty Opponents in Kentucky Prepare for Clemency Push Earlier than Planned
author: Lauren Gill
content:
Opponents of the death penalty are asking Kentucky’s governor to commute the
sentences of people on death row before he leaves office late next year. But
their timetable was upended last week when voters approved new limits on a
governor’s ability to grant clemency late in their term.

Under the change, governors are prohibited from issuing pardons, reprieves, or
commutations starting 60 days before an election and until the end of their
term. The Kentucky legislature put the proposal on the ballot via bipartisan
majorities this spring, and 71 percent of Kentuckians approved the
constitutional amendment last week.

Proponents of the amendment argued that it will stop governors from waiting
until the end of their term to grant clemency to dodge political consequences.
“Do not wait until electoral accountability has effectively disappeared,”
Senator Chris McDaniel, a Republican who [sponsored the
measure](https://kentuckylantern.com/2026/06/01/with-legislature-on-board-at-
last-kentuckians-will-vote-on-pardon-limits-amid-elections/), warned in the
[_Northern Kentucky Tribune_ last
month](https://nkytribune.com/2026/10/opinion-chris-mcdaniel-vote-yes-on-
constitutional-amendment-on-governors-pardoning-powers/).

McDaniel, who did not reply to a request for comment, has said he drafted the
amendment in direct response to the controversy that erupted in late 2019 when
Republican Governor Matt Bevin issued over 400 pardons and commutations on his
way out of office. Bevin came under heavy fire over [corruption
allegations](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/matt-bevin-pardons-convicted-
killers-granted-relief-by-outgoing-kentucky-governor-today-2019-12-13/)
related to his pardon of Patrick Baker, whose family [hosted a
fundraiser](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/matt-bevin-pardons-convicted-killers-
granted-relief-by-outgoing-kentucky-governor-today-2019-12-13/) for Bevin that
raised $21,500. Bevin also faced criticism for his decisions to grant clemency
to people convicted of violent crimes, [some of
whom](https://www.cnn.com/2020/04/10/us/kentucky-man-pardoned-arrest-child-
pornography) ended up [back in
prison](https://www.kentucky.com/news/local/crime/article291370655.html).

Governor Andy Beshear, a Democrat, will now be the first governor constrained
by this rule. It means he has only until early September of next year to issue
clemency instead of until the end of his term in December 2027.

Russell Allen, executive director of the Kentucky Coalition to Abolish the
Death Penalty, is concerned that executions could resume in Kentucky should
Republicans take office next year and he believes Beshear could preempt that
by removing people from death row, much like [Joe Biden
did](https://boltsmag.org/death-row-clemency-adx-supermax/) ahead of Donald
Trump’s return to power in 2024. He told _Bolts_ that the amendment made the
group's campaign to convince Beshear to commute the sentences of all 23 people
on the state’s death row even more pressing.

“It definitely gives us a sense of urgency, and we want Governor Beshear to
have that same sense of urgency when he starts to look at these cases,” said
Allen.

Allen’s efforts in Kentucky mirror similar blitzes elsewhere at the end of a
governor’s term, as opponents of the death penalty make the case that the
death penalty is applied unfairly and that failing to commute the row could
leave the door open to renewed executions under a new governor. The [largest
grant](https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/illinois-commutations-twenty-years-ago-
marked-turning-point-in-death-penalty-abolition) of death row clemency in
modern history came in early 2003 in Illinois, when then-Governor George Ryan
commuted the sentence of all 167 people on death row to life without parole
just two days before he was to leave office.

Oregon Governor Kate Brown [also emptied](https://boltsmag.org/death-penalty-
and-clemency-oregon-nevada/) her state’s death row in 2022, less than a month
before the end of her term. Under Kentucky’s new rules, neither Ryan nor Brown
would have been allowed to make those decisions at that point of their terms.

Other recent governors have faced similar pressure. As he prepared to leave
office in 2024, North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper faced a [multiyear campaign
to get him to](https://boltsmag.org/north-carolina-death-penalty-mass-
clemency-roy-cooper/) commute the sentences of 136 people but he only ended up
commuting the sentences of [15](https://governor.nc.gov/news/press-
releases/2024/12/31/governor-cooper-takes-capital-clemency-actions)—on the
final day of his term. And [Louisiana activists](https://boltsmag.org/the-
death-penalty-on-trial-in-louisiana/) in 2023 made a comparable push before
then-Governor John Bel Edwards, a Democrat, left office and was replaced by
current Governor Jeff Landry, a Republican death penalty supporter, but they
were foiled in part by Louisiana’s complex rules for clemency, which requires
a board’s approval. Landry then promptly resumed executions after a quarter-
century hiatus.

In California last week, Governor Gavin Newsom [announced he would
seek](https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/11/gavin-newsom-death-penalty-
commutation/) to commute the sentences of the state’s 548 death row
prisoners—the largest death row in the nation—to life without the possibility
of parole. (California’s supreme court must still approve the majority of
those commutations.)

Newsom is a possible candidate for president in 2028, [as is
Beshear](https://www.wlky.com/article/beshear-presidential-run-kentucky-
answer-thursday/74347601), and their approaches to the death penalty could be
an issue in Democratic primaries.

So far, Beshear’s [use of clemency](https://www.kentucky.gov/Pages/Activity-
stream.aspx?n=GovernorBeshear&prId=2774&m=180.95238095238)—a power that lies
solely with him, unlike in Louisiana and some other states—has been limited to
[posthumous pardons](https://www.kentucky.gov/Pages/Activity-
stream.aspx?n=GovernorBeshear&prId=2774&m=180.95238095238) of 43 people who
helped slaves escape to freedom. He opposed Amendment 1, saying that his
predecessor used his power in “terrible ways” but that voters shouldn’t let
that constrain the future. He [told the state press in
October](https://www.wate.com/news/kentucky/governor-beshear-weighs-in-on-
proposed-change-to-kentuckys-constitution/?nxsparam=4), “The answer to this
isn’t changing the pardon power of every other governor that hasn’t abused it
this way, but not electing a guy like Matt Bevin ever again.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/73273979_2637375146378780_5327791632290938880_n.jpg)_Controversy
around pardons then-Governor Matt Bevin issued in late 2019 helped fuel the
push for Amendment 1, according to a sponsor (photo via Bevin for
Governor/Facebook)_

In Kentucky, the death penalty has laid dormant due to a 2010 order by local
judge Phillip Shepherd, a [frequent foil](https://boltsmag.org/judicial-
election-and-voting-rights-in-franklin-kentucky/) of Kentucky conservatives,
who [blocked executions](https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/kentucky-judge-rules-
against-lethal-injection-protocol-and-halts-execution) in part over concerns
with the state’s execution protocols. The litigation over those protocols has
continued in Shepherd’s courtroom since then, including [as recently as this
summer](https://www.lpm.org/news/2026-08-20/kentucky-supreme-court-denies-
latest-attempt-to-halt-execution-protocols-challenge).

As a result, there hasn’t been an execution since 2008. Also, no one has been
sentenced to death in the state since 2014.

But some Republicans in the state are working to change that. Attorney General
Russell Coleman petitioned the Kentucky Supreme Court to force Shepperd to
lift his injunction and allow state officials to schedule an execution, but
the supreme court has
[repeatedly](https://www.lpm.org/news/2026-08-20/kentucky-supreme-court-
denies-latest-attempt-to-halt-execution-protocols-challenge)
[rebuffed](https://www.lex18.com/news/covering-kentucky/kentucky-supreme-
court-denies-ag-request-in-death-penalty-dispute)
[Coleman](https://www.lex18.com/news/covering-kentucky/kentucky-supreme-court-
denies-ag-request-in-death-penalty-dispute)’s efforts this year. Also this
year, the GOP-run legislature [overrode a
veto](https://www.lex18.com/news/covering-kentucky/kentucky-supreme-court-
denies-ag-request-in-death-penalty-dispute) by Beshear to [pass
legislation](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/26rs/sb251.html) that
expedites the Kentucky Department of Corrections’ drafting of execution
procedures by allowing the agency to skip the public rulemaking process,
making it easier to resume executions.

Coleman is running for reelection next year. Republicans also hope to win back
the governor’s office since Beshear is term-limited from running for
reelection. One of the Republican frontrunners in the governor’s race, U.S.
Representative James Comer, has
[styled](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/house/3108669/comer-opens-
inquiry-into-9-11-plea-deals-questions-lack-of-
transparency/?srsltid=AYCX9vL55CbMlCqrdm6sEfN2ah_U6ynFPB9CcdVrz_0fT89s9UL0lbcS)
himself a champion of the death penalty.

Along with the new guardrails created by Amendment 1, the push for Beshear to
clear death row “becomes even more important now because of the fact that he
is leaving the state in an unsure place,” said Allen.

He explained that that he plans to make the case to Beshear that there are
people on death row who could be innocent or otherwise shouldn’t be there
because of issues such as intellectual disability

Tim Arnold, an attorney who has worked on clemency petitions at the Kentucky
Department of Public Advocacy, the state’s public defense arm, is critical of
the amendment.

One of his chief concerns is that the new rule would bar death row prisoners
from asking that the governor spare their lives via a commutation or reprieve
if their execution happens to be scheduled during the restricted time period.

That would mean that some people about to be executed have access to a common
reprieve mechanism while others do not, and Arnold says this could violate
their rights. The courts “might feel that there's a kind of a due process
issue if what's happening is everybody else can get it, but this group of
people in this time frame cannot,” he said.

With Amendment 1’s passage, Kentucky becomes the only state that places time
restrictions on commutations and pardons, according to Mark Osler, a law
professor at the University of St. Thomas and an expert on clemency. He is
optimistic about the change, saying that the amendment could force governors
to be more deliberate about their choices. “There's a rush of them at the end,
and it's hard to believe that they're carefully thought out,” he said. “It’s
something that I think is intended to be considered regularly.”

Allen told _Bolts_ that the Kentucky Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty
will launch its campaign, “Do the Right Thing Andy,” in January. He’s hoping
that as Beshear contemplates higher office he’ll be inspired by the Democratic
momentum from last week’s midterms.

He said, “We think that commuting Kentucky's death row is a large signal that
he believes in a new world and he's actually putting boots to ground to try to
make it happen.”
